analysis.one_liner: Requires car makers to share repair information, tools, and parts with independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: A bill to force car makers to share repair information with independent shops and car owners won 54 cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require car manufacturers to sell or give all repair information, diagnostic tools, and replacement equipment to car owners and independent repair shops on the same terms they give their own dealers. It would let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the requirement and allow state attorneys general, consumers, and repair shops to sue violators. It had bipartisan support but was referred to committee and never heard again.
analysis.who_benefits: Car owners who want to fix or maintain their vehicles at independent shops, the independent repair shops that could service more cars, and the aftermarket tool and parts industry. The bill's findings cite a survey where 14 percent of consumers were turned away from an independent shop that lacked the needed tools or information [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to provide vehicle owners and all service providers the information needed to diagnose, service, maintain, or repair a vehicle, on reasonable and non-discriminatory terms [S3].
Requires manufacturers to sell diagnostic tools and equipment to consumers and independent shops, and to share the information needed for aftermarket tool companies to make equivalent tools [S3].
Lets the FTC treat a violation as an unfair or deceptive practice, and lets state attorneys general, consumers, and service providers sue for injunctions or damages [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Car manufacturers, who would have to disclose repair information and sell tools and replacement equipment that they currently reserve for their own dealer networks, which could reduce the service revenue that flows to franchised dealers.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers argued that opening their diagnostic systems could expose trade secrets and safety-critical software; the bill responds by exempting trade secrets only if they are not shared with authorized dealers [S3], but drafting that line in practice would have been contentious.
Independent shops and aftermarket companies already provide most repairs; critics could argue the mandate imposes compliance costs on manufacturers for a problem the market largely handled.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real barrier — some independent shops lacked the information or tools to service newer computer-controlled vehicles — and had a narrow, enforcement-based design. The cost to manufacturers would have been real but modest relative to the value of a competitive repair market, and the trade secret carve-out shows the drafters anticipated the main objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee in June 2007, and no further action was taken before that Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 13, 2007, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, where it stayed with no hearings, markups, or floor action for the remainder of the 110th Congress [S5].
It attracted 54 cosponsors, 48 Democrats and 6 Republicans, but never advanced beyond committee referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Car manufacturers and their dealer networks, which kept exclusive control of repair information, tools, and equipment for their vehicles for another Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Car makers and their dealer networks

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and did not hold a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended

against.name: Auto manufacturers and dealer networks
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would expose trade secrets and shift repair work away from franchised dealers

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was 48 Democrats and 6 Republicans, so support skewed Democratic but was not strictly partisan; the bill died without a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their exclusive control of repair information, tools, and equipment, and allowed independent shops to compete for repair revenue that currently flows to dealer service departments.
The bill would have given them the information and tools to service computer-controlled vehicles they currently cannot fully repair, expanding their customer base.

The bill would have required manufacturers to share the information needed for aftermarket companies to build equivalent tools, and the findings note the aftermarket already employs over 5 million workers and generates about $200 billion in annual sales [S3].
